atproto.description: Proves you control a Bluesky (AT Protocol) account: approve on your server, and Ghostly publishes one record in your account's repository. It is public, like the rest of your repository: anyone can see this account made a Ghostly proof, not who you share it with. Contacts check it without logging in.
atproto.limits: Signed with your account's key, which your server usually holds. It proves control of the account, not who you are; the handle is shown only while it points back to the account.
atproto.privacy: Your contact's app asks the PLC directory (or your did:web host) for your account's document, your server for the record, and its DNS-over-HTTPS resolver or your handle's website for your handle, so they learn this account was checked.

handle.help: Your Bluesky handle, your own domain if you use one, or your DID.

atproto-oauth-full.label: Your server, full access (older servers)

bitcoin.description: Proves you can sign with the key behind a Bitcoin address: your wallet signs the statement and you paste the signature.
bitcoin.label: Bitcoin address
bitcoin.limits: It does not prove a balance, a past payment, or that you would pay.

paste.label: Signature
paste.placeholder: smp… (BIP-322) or the base64 signature your wallet shows

bitcoin.privacy: Nothing: the signature is checked on this device, with no blockchain lookup. Contacts you share it with learn the address.

bitcoin-core.description: Legacy message signature: for a legacy 1… address only.

electrum.description: Legacy message signature: for a legacy 1… address only.

trezor.description: Legacy message signature: for a legacy 1… address only.

steps.cannotSign: {{wallet}} cannot sign for a {{type}} address in a format Ghostly accepts. Use a wallet that signs BIP-322.
steps.cannotSignTry: {{wallet}} cannot sign for a {{type}} address in a format Ghostly accepts. Try {{others}}, or another wallet that signs BIP-322.
steps.limits: This shows you can sign for the address. It does not show a balance, a past payment, or that you would pay.
steps.statement: Sign exactly this statement, as one line, without adding a line break:

subject.help: Proves: whoever made this signature could sign with the key behind this address when they signed. Does not prove the address holds any balance, now or ever. Does not prove they sent or received any past payment. Does not prove they would pay you, or spend from this address at all.
subject.label: Bitcoin address

bitcoin.summary: Sign a message in your own wallet

bitcoin-core.step1: Bitcoin Core signs messages in the legacy format only, for a legacy address (1… on mainnet, m… or n… on test networks). Make one in the Receive tab with the Base58 (Legacy) type, or with `getnewaddress "" legacy`.
bitcoin-core.step2: GUI: File → Sign message…; paste the address, paste the statement, Sign Message, copy the signature.
bitcoin-core.step3: Command line: bitcoin-cli signmessage "<address>" '<statement>' (single quotes keep the statement's double quotes intact).
bitcoin-core.testnet: Run it with -signet, -testnet4 or -regtest; add the same flag to bitcoin-cli.

coldcard.note: Older firmware signs only the legacy format (Ghostly accepts that for a legacy 1… address) and limits message length and characters.
coldcard.step1: Follow COLDCARD's BIP-322 guide for your firmware: it signs the statement for one of its addresses via MicroSD, NFC or QR, depending on the model.
coldcard.step2: Give it the statement exactly as Ghostly shows it and the address you are proving.
coldcard.step3: Paste the signature it produces into Ghostly.

electrum.step1: Electrum signs in the legacy format, which Ghostly accepts only for a legacy 1… address (m…/n… on test networks); its default bc1… wallets need another wallet.
electrum.step2: Addresses tab (View → Show Addresses), right-click the address → Sign/verify message.
electrum.step3: Paste the statement into Message, click Sign, copy the Signature and paste it into Ghostly.

other.step1: Look for "Sign message" in the wallet. Choose BIP-322 when it asks for a format.
other.step2: Sign the statement exactly as Ghostly shows it, with the address you are proving.
other.step3: A nested SegWit address (3…, or 2… on test networks) needs a full BIP-322 signature (it starts with ful…).
other.step4: Paste the signature into Ghostly; it tells you right away if it does not match.

sparrow.note: Sparrow offers BIP322 (Simple) for software wallets only; a connected hardware wallet signs the Standard (Electrum) format, which Ghostly accepts only for a legacy 1… address.
sparrow.step1: Open the wallet that holds the address, then Tools → Sign/Verify Message.
sparrow.step2: Address: paste the address you are proving.
sparrow.step3: Message: paste the statement Ghostly shows, exactly as it is.
sparrow.step4: Format: BIP322 (Simple) for a bc1q… or bc1p… address (tb1… on test networks). For a legacy 1… address, Standard (Electrum).
sparrow.step5: Sign Message, then copy the whole Signature (it starts with smp…) and paste it into Ghostly.
sparrow.testnet: Tools → Restart In → Testnet or Signet, with a wallet on that network.

trezor.step1: Trezor signs messages in the legacy format; Ghostly accepts it for an address of a Legacy account (1…).
trezor.step2: Open the Legacy account and choose Sign & verify in its menu.
trezor.step3: Paste the statement into Message, pick the address, Sign, confirm on the device, copy the signature into Ghostly.

domain.description: Proves you control a domain name: publish a DNS TXT record or a file on its website, once. Contacts' apps look it up when you share it and can check again later.

dns.name: Open the DNS settings of {{domain}} at your registrar or DNS host and add a TXT record with this name. Some hosts add the domain themselves: then enter only the part before {{domain}}.
dns.public: The record stays public while the proof is in use. Removing it withdraws this proof from every contact at their next check.
dns.ttl: Set the TTL to 300 seconds or less, so removing the record takes effect quickly. Then press Check: DNS changes can take a few minutes to appear.

https.check: Then press Check. The file stays public while the proof is in use; deleting it withdraws this proof from every contact at their next check.

domain.limits: Does not prove who runs the domain, only that whoever added the proof could publish under it.

domain.privacy: DNS: the contact's app asks the DNS-over-HTTPS resolver chosen in its settings (Quad9 by default; the next of Quad9, Cloudflare and Google when it cannot be reached) for the record, so that resolver learns the domain was checked. Website or NIP-05: the resolver learns the domain, and the domain's web server sees the contact's IP address.

approval.googleNote: An identity Passport makes with Google is recovered with Google plus Passport: both are needed, neither alone can.
approval.passportAbout: Opens Pubky Passport. No Passport identity yet? It offers “Continue with Google” and makes one.
approval.qrNote: The code is your request: scan it yourself, and do not share it.

pubky.description: Proves you hold a Pubky key: approve one request in Pubky Ring or Pubky Passport, and Ghostly writes a small proof file to your homeserver. Contacts’ apps read it back through your key’s own records.
pubky.limits: The file is on your homeserver: whoever runs it could write there too. It does not prove who holds the key.
pubky.privacy: Your contact’s app reads your key’s records from Pubky’s Pkarr relays (pkarr.pubky.org, pkarr.pubky.app), looks up your homeserver’s address through its DNS-over-HTTPS resolver (or the next one when that cannot be reached; it only contacts a public address, on port 443), and reads the proof file from your homeserver, which sees the contact’s IP address.

progress.deleting: Deleting the proof file from your homeserver…
progress.popupBlocked: Your browser blocked the Passport window: allow pop-ups for Ghostly and press the button again, or scan the code with Pubky Ring.
progress.writing: Writing the proof to your homeserver…

pubky-auth.description: One request: approve it in Pubky Passport in your browser, or scan it with Pubky Ring. Ghostly only asks to write one small file to a new folder of your homeserver.
pubky-auth.label: Pubky Ring or Pubky Passport

subject.help: Comes from Pubky Ring or Passport when you approve.
subject.label: Pubky key

pubky.summary: Approve in Pubky Ring or Passport

unpublish.description: Also deletes the proof file on your homeserver: that takes one more approval in Pubky Ring or Passport, since Ghostly kept no access to it.

ssh.description: Proves you hold an SSH key, including FIDO security keys: sign the statement once with ssh-keygen and paste the signature.
ssh.label: SSH key
ssh.privacy: Nothing: the signature is checked on this device. The key's fingerprint links every chat you share it in.

ssh-keygen.description: Sign with OpenSSH's ssh-keygen (8.1 or later): a key file, ssh-agent, or a FIDO security key.

steps.orSave: Or save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.
steps.paste: Paste the whole signature it prints, from -----BEGIN SSH SIGNATURE----- to -----END SSH SIGNATURE-----. Your private key never leaves your computer.
steps.run: Run this in a terminal (macOS, Linux, or Git Bash/WSL on Windows). If your key is not ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, change the path after -f; a .pub path works when the private key is in ssh-agent or on a security key.
steps.save: Save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.

subject.help: Your public key, the one line in the .pub file. Contacts see its fingerprint.
subject.label: Public key

ssh-github.description: Proves you hold an SSH key your GitHub account publishes: sign the statement once with ssh-keygen. No GitHub login.
ssh-github.label: GitHub (SSH key)
ssh-github.limits: Does not prove a GitHub login: only that a key the account lists is yours, for as long as it stays listed.
ssh-github.privacy: Your contact's app asks api.github.com for this account's public SSH keys, when you share it and on each re-check: GitHub learns the account was looked up, and from which IP address. So does this app when you add it.

ssh-keygen.description: Sign with an SSH key that your GitHub account lists (Settings → SSH keys).

steps.orSave: Or save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.
steps.paste: Paste the whole signature it prints, from -----BEGIN SSH SIGNATURE----- to -----END SSH SIGNATURE-----. Your private key never leaves your computer.
steps.run: Run this in a terminal (macOS, Linux, or Git Bash/WSL on Windows). If your key is not ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, change the path after -f; a .pub path works when the private key is in ssh-agent or on a security key.
steps.save: Save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.

ssh-github.summary: A key your GitHub account lists

ssh-gitlab.description: Proves you hold an SSH key your GitLab account publishes: sign the statement once with ssh-keygen. No GitLab login.
ssh-gitlab.label: GitLab (SSH key)
ssh-gitlab.limits: Does not prove a GitLab login: only that a key the account lists is yours, for as long as it stays listed.
ssh-gitlab.privacy: Your contact's app asks gitlab.com for this account's public SSH keys, when you share it and on each re-check: GitLab learns the account was looked up, and from which IP address. So does this app when you add it.

ssh-keygen.description: Sign with an SSH key that your GitLab account lists (Settings → SSH keys).

steps.orSave: Or save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.
steps.paste: Paste the whole signature it prints, from -----BEGIN SSH SIGNATURE----- to -----END SSH SIGNATURE-----. Your private key never leaves your computer.
steps.run: Run this in a terminal (macOS, Linux, or Git Bash/WSL on Windows). If your key is not ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, change the path after -f; a .pub path works when the private key is in ssh-agent or on a security key.
steps.save: Save this statement to a file, run ssh-keygen -Y sign -n {{namespace}} -f <your key> <file>, and paste the <file>.sig it writes.

ssh-gitlab.summary: A key your GitLab account lists
